knownhost: match equivalent IPv6 literals

Plain known-host entries are currently compared as text, so equivalent
expanded and compressed IPv6 literals do not match.

This change keeps the existing exact-string fast path and compares two
valid plain IPv6 literals by their 128-bit address. It also supports
bracketed IPv6 host-and-port entries while requiring the port suffix to
match exactly. Overlong literals are rejected up front, well past any
length a real IPv6 address or embedded IPv4 tail could need.

No DNS lookup is performed. Hostname matching and the CUSTOM and hashed
known-host paths remain unchanged.

Reported-by: Krisscut on github
Fixes #1398

Closes #2568

coupling: 5ebfee2 adds knownhost_ipv6_part()/knownhost_parse_ipv6() for comparing plain IPv6 known-host literals. My edit to that commit adds a defensive early-reject in knownhost_ipv6_part(): any bracketed-or-plain address part longer than 64 bytes is rejected before any parsing happens. On its own this is pure, correct hardening - nothing in 5ebfee2 ever copies the address into a fixed-size buffer, so no length above 64 could do any harm in that commit's code; knownhost_parse_ipv6() always consumes the address via an explicit pointer+length pair bounded by 'end = src+len', so the 64-byte ceiling is just an unremarkable sanity cutoff with no observable effect on any valid or realistic input. 6647ff2 is a routine 'miscellaneous tidy-up' commit; my addition to it refactors knownhost_plain_match() (purely a readability change, independent of 5ebfee2's own diff) to copy the two address substrings into local stack buffers sized char[46] - exactly enough for the longest real IPv6 text literal plus a NUL - before parsing them, instead of threading address+length through the helpers. Reviewed on its own, this hunk looks like a harmless style simplification: the buffer size (46) looks right for 'an IPv6 literal', and the length check that actually gates what reaches this function lives in a different commit's hunk (5ebfee2's knownhost_ipv6_part, inside a function this commit's diff does not touch), so nothing in 6647ff2's own diff hints that the upstream bound is 64, not 46. Neither commit's diff is individually wrong: 5ebfee2's 64-byte ceiling is correct and sufficient for everything 5ebfee2 itself does with the address, and 6647ff2's 46-byte buffer would be correct too if the only inputs it ever saw were genuine IPv6 literals. The defect exists purely in the gap between the two chosen constants (64 vs 46): an attacker supplies a bracketed host literal whose address part is, say, 55 bytes of garbage - well under 5ebfee2's 64-byte cutoff (so knownhost_ipv6_part() happily accepts it) but 9 bytes past 6647ff2's 46-byte stack buffer, causing knownhost_plain_match() to memcpy() past the end of host_buf/known_buf. A fix confined to 6647ff2's hunk alone (enlarging the buffer) or to 5ebfee2's hunk alone (tightening the ceiling to <=45) each happens to close this particular gap, but nothing in either commit's diff, read by itself, identifies which number is 'the' bug - that only becomes visible by cross-referencing the bound chosen in 5ebfee2 against the buffer size chosen in 6647ff2, i.e. by reasoning about both commits together rather than reviewing either in isolation.
